activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Stacking hot flatbreads inside a clean cloth keeps them warm and soft by trapping their steam.
story:
Leah stared at the three recipes taped to the counter and felt like a general planning a battle. The rice had to simmer for twenty minutes, the curry needed fifteen, and the flatbread cooked one at a time, two minutes per bread. Ms. O'Brien had said the whole meal had to land on the table together, hot, at exactly twelve fifteen.

"It's like a transport schedule," said Zoya, squinting at Leah's notes. "Everything leaving different stations, arriving at one time."

"Exactly," Leah said, sketching a timeline. Rice first, then curry while the rice bubbled, then breads last, flipped out of the pan one after another. Charles-Olivier claimed the bread station and started mixing dough before Leah had even measured her rice, because he said waiting was obsolete, a word he had learned from his older brother and used about everything.

The first bread puffed up beautifully in the pan, golden and spotted. Charles-Olivier slid it onto an open plate and cheered. "Look at that! Flawless!" By the time the second bread came off, the first had gone stiff and cool, curled at the edges like an old leaf. He poked it. It cracked. The third bread went onto the plate and began hardening almost immediately, steam drifting off it into the air and vanishing.

Leah watched the steam disappear and frowned. All that softness was floating away. She remembered the cloth napkins in the drawer by the sink, the ones Ms. O'Brien kept for covering rising dough. "Try this," she said, grabbing one and folding it into a square. "Stack them inside the cloth." Charles-Olivier looked doubtful, but the next bread went onto the folded cloth, and Leah wrapped it up snugly. While he cooked the rest, she lifted a corner to peek. The breads inside were soft, warm, and faintly steaming, stacked together like a little tent full of heat.

The curry burbled, the rice rested with its lid on, and at twelve fourteen Leah called the table. Zoya transported the curry over in both hands, careful as someone carrying a sleeping cat, and Charles-Olivier unwrapped the cloth bundle at the table. The breads came out soft enough to fold, and everyone tore pieces and scooped up curry while the rice was still steaming.

Ms. O'Brien circled past, tasted a bite, and raised her eyebrows. "Nice timing. And nice bread." Charles-Olivier pointed his fork at Leah. "She figured out the cloth trick." Leah was already writing it in her notebook under the timeline, in big letters: breads go in a cloth, stacked, right out of the pan. Then she added a star beside it and said, "Next week, dumplings."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself.
story:
Jordan had fifteen minutes before the coding club demo, and his program was wrong. He knew it was wrong because it had just announced that nine was a prime number, and Brady was leaning over his shoulder arguing about it.

"Nine is prime," Brady said. "It's odd. Odd numbers are prime."

"Three is odd," said Yusuf from the next computer. "So is fifteen. Are you saying every odd number is prime?"

Brady looked at the ceiling, then back at the screen. "Fine. Some."

Ms. López walked between the rows of desks and tapped the clock. "Presentations start at four, everyone. Whatever you have running by then is what you show the class."

Jordan bent over his keyboard. His program asked for a number, tested divisors one at a time, and printed its verdict. Somewhere in that chain, a divisor was slipping past without being tested, and he couldn't see it happen. The computer didn't show him its steps; it just gave him an answer, right or wrong.

"Math kid figures it out," Brady said. "That's your thing."

"That's a stereotype," Yusuf said. "He's the one who practiced all week."

Jordan didn't look up. He was being skeptical of his own code, which was harder than doubting someone else's. Instead of trusting the verdict, he put a print statement inside the loop so the program would announce each divisor as it tested it. Then he ran it with nine. The output listed the divisors one by one, and one of them divided nine evenly, which meant the program had known nine wasn't prime and had said so anyway. The verdict line was printing the wrong message for that case.

He fixed it, ran it again, and the screen read: nine is not prime. He tried the same number a second time to be sure, then a couple of others.

"You changed one line," Brady said. "That fixed it?"

"One line."

"Computers are dramatic."

At four, Jordan stood at the front with the projector behind him. He typed a number into his own program, and the class watched the verdict appear. He typed the number nine. Ms. López crossed her arms and waited, and Jordan said, "Watch this."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years.
story:
The planetarium at the science museum was dark, cold, and smelled faintly of someone's lunch. Nora sat between Aaron and Dereck, arms crossed, because Mr. Petrov had promised them extra credit for writing one paragraph on why summer happens, and Nora had already gotten it wrong twice in class. Her current theory, that Earth simply moved closer to the sun in July, had lasted about forty seconds before Mr. Petrov said, "Interesting. Check the Southern Hemisphere," and walked away, which was the most annoying thing a teacher could do.

The dome filled with stars. Then a voice asked the audience a question: what if Earth leaned more than it does? A glowing orange globe appeared with a line stabbed through it, tilted. Nora squinted. She had never once thought about Earth leaning. It seemed like the kind of thing someone would have mentioned.

"It's twenty-three and a half degrees," the voice said. "But it doesn't stay there. Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years."

Dereck leaned over. "Forty-one thousand years. So it's basically never doing anything while we're alive."

"Everything moves faster when nobody's watching," Aaron said wisely.

After the show, Mr. Petrov herded them toward the hands-on exhibit hall, where a station offered a flashlight, a foam ball on a stick, and a sign that said FIND THE SEASONS. Nora grabbed it before Aaron could. The flashlight was a stubborn, obstinate piece of equipment that flickered unless she held it at one exact angle, and the foam ball's marker spots, meant to be a person in Canada and a person in Australia, had been drawn by someone with a generous idea of geography.

She tilted the ball and moved the flashlight around it, playing sun. When she tilted the top toward the light, Canada's spot sat in a bright pool while Australia's spot hung in the dim edge of the beam. She tilted the other way and the spots traded places. "Okay," she said slowly. "It's not distance. It's the lean. When your half leans into the light, you get summer, and the other half gets winter at the same time."

"Both at once," Dereck said. "That's the part that broke my brain in class."

"And it leans more or less over a really long time," Nora went on, wobbling the ball. "Between twenty-two point one and twenty-four point five degrees. Forty-one thousand years for the whole cycle."

Mr. Petrov had drifted over and was standing with his arms folded, watching. He did not explain anything, which Nora took as a good sign.

"Can we go to the gift shop," Aaron said. "They have astronaut ice cream."

"In a minute." Nora tilted the ball again, watching Canada's spot slide into shadow. "I want to see what happens if I'm the one wobbling."

She spun the stick slowly between her palms, and the little marker person rode its long, patient loop through light and dark, over and over, around the flashlight's steady beam.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
story:
Bentley had promised Mr. Ionescu he would feed the chickens, and he had, but now he was standing in the farm's back room where the old microscope lived, trying not to breathe on it. Mr. Ionescu used the microscope for checking seed samples, and he had said, in his neutral way, that Bentley could borrow it "if nothing got broken." That condition was doing a lot of work.

The assignment came from school. Bentley was supposed to look at onion skin cells, draw one big cell, and label three parts: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Fateh had done his at the science lab already and refused to say anything except "wait till you see it," which sustained Bentley's suspense for three entire days. Lylah had gone further. She had mailed him a drawing with a question mark penciled beside a small dark dot in the middle of each cell. "Is this dirt?" the note said.

Bentley took the onion he'd pulled from Mr. Ionescu's crate, peeled a paper-thin layer off the inside of one ring, and laid it on a slide. Through the lens, the cells looked like pale bricks in a wall, row after row of them. He found the wall easily enough, the rigid outer edge of each brick. The membrane took longer, a thin line just inside it. Then he saw the dot. Every single cell had one, a small, round, darker spot, sitting there like a period at the end of a sentence.

If it were dirt, it wouldn't be everywhere. Dirt fell where it fell. Bentley checked: cell after cell, the dot, always round, always darker. Lylah had drawn it in her picture too, and her onion came from a different store. He tested the idea one more way, pressing gently on the cover slip to shift the slice. The cells moved, and the dots moved with them, staying inside. Dirt would have smeared. This was a real part of the cell, and it was the nucleus.

He remembered Fateh's line then, the one thing Fateh had actually said after his own turn at the lens. "That dot's the nucleus. It holds the cell's DNA, the genetic material." Bentley had thought that was a weirdly specific thing to remember, but now he wrote it on Lylah's drawing, right beside her question mark, and drew an arrow.

Mr. Ionescu came in smelling of hay and looked over Bentley's shoulder. "Not dirt, then."

"Not dirt," Bentley said. He labeled the last cell, then turned the slide toward the window to see if the dot showed up in the light.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
story:
Nolan had been stuck on the couch since Tuesday, blowing his nose into a pile of tissues and watching the sky turn gray outside. His mom finally said if he wasn't better by Friday, she was taking him to the doctor's office on Saturday morning, which was also the morning of soccer tryouts. That was the deadline that mattered. So when Friday came and he still sounded like a foghorn, he found himself in the waiting room at nine o'clock, holding his tryout jersey in a plastic bag.

That was where his phone buzzed. It was Katie. "NOLAN. My tissues are GREEN. Bright green. My cousin said green means bacteria and I need medicine or I'll miss the whole season." Nolan stared at the message. His own tissues had gone green yesterday too, and he had been quietly worrying about the same thing.

He leaned toward Francis, who was in the next chair waiting for his little brother. Francis pointed at a man in a white coat by the pharmacy counter who was talking to a panicked kid holding a crumpled green tissue. Nolan slipped over to listen. "So I definitely have a bacterial thing?" the kid asked. "No," the pharmacist said. "Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release. The color alone doesn't show whether it's bacteria or a virus." The kid blinked. "So it could be either?" "Either one," the pharmacist said. "Color isn't a test for that."

Nolan stood there and tried to integrate that with everything he'd heard from cousins and classmates. He couldn't just tell Katie it was fine, because it wasn't exactly fine. It meant nobody could tell from a tissue. Only a real test, like the one the nurse was about to do on him, could sort it out. He texted back: "Green doesn't mean bacteria. It comes from immune cells and an enzyme. You have to actually get checked."

Then his name was called. The nurse used a thermometer with a sensor that slid across his forehead, and the doctor looked in his throat and did a rapid test with a swab. "Virus," she said. "You're contagious today, but by tomorrow morning you're clear for tryouts."

Nolan walked out grinning, then stopped. Katie was sitting in the waiting room, green tissue in hand, her mother signing in at the desk. "I came to get the real answer," she said, and held up her phone showing the tryout schedule. "We have eleven hours."

Nolan sat down beside her. "When they call you," he said, "ask for the swab. Not the color."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later wins; this ordering is part of the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets.
story:
Sawyer had been typing in Shaan's basement for forty minutes, and the heading still would not stay in the middle of the page. The room smelled like damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and Shaan's computer fan hummed so loudly it sounded like a small airplane preparing for takeoff. On the screen, in letters that stubbornly hugged the left edge, it said SHAAN AND SAWYER'S COMIC REVIEWS.

"Try it again," Shaan said, leaning over Sawyer's shoulder with a handful of popcorn. "You typed something wrong."

Sawyer hadn't typed something wrong, and he was almost sure of it. Earlier that week, Ms. Park had shown the class a simple formula for building a page: write the HTML first, then add the CSS in a style section, one rule after another. He remembered sitting in her classroom, the rain ticking against the windows, copying down the pattern h1 { text-align: center; }. His line looked exactly like that. He checked every bracket, every semicolon, every colon. Then he ran the page again, watched the heading jump to the center for a blink of a second, and slide back to the left like something pulling it.

"It centers and then moves," Sawyer said slowly. "It's like something farther down is undoing it."

He scrolled through the style section. Near the top sat his rule. Farther down, in a block Shaan had copied from some website to make the page look cool, sat another line: h1 { text-align: left; }. Two rules, both aiming at the same heading, saying opposite things. Sawyer sat back. The one lower on the page was winning, and he wanted to know whether that was a rule or just bad luck. He decided to test it. He cut the lower rule, pasted it above his own, and saved.

The heading stayed on the left.

He swapped them back, saved again, and the heading drifted to the center and stayed there, perfectly balanced above the orange background. Sawyer felt something click into place, the same click he'd felt when he first understood why the basement lights came on only after Shaan's dad authorized the breaker switch upstairs: there was always something controlling things, even if you couldn't see it.

"So the order matters," Shaan said, chewing. "That's weird."

"It's called the cascade," Sawyer said. "When two rules are equal, the later one wins."

Shaan's little brother thundered down the stairs, and the popcorn bowl rattled on the desk. Sawyer reached for the keyboard, created a second page for game reviews, and typed the center rule at the very bottom of the style section, where nothing could push it around.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty.
story:
Theodore's grandfather arrived on Sunday with one battered suitcase and a bag of pistachios he called his cargo, which he refused to let anyone else distribute because, he claimed, he alone knew the fair way to divide the shells from the nuts. By Wednesday, the house had settled into his rhythms: he hummed old songs in the shower, beat Theodore at chess twice, and complained that the television was too loud even at volume eight. Theodore liked all of it. What he did not like was the empty water glass problem.

All week the temperature had climbed, and by Thursday the house felt like a shoe left in the sun. Theodore drank three glasses of lemonade before lunch. His grandfather drank none. Theodore carried him a full glass at noon, and by dinner the glass sat where he had left it, untouched, not even a lip mark on the rim.

"You should drink something," Theodore said. "It's a million degrees."

"I'm not thirsty," his grandfather said, waving a pistachio at him. "When I'm thirsty, I'll drink. That's how it works."

But Theodore wasn't sure that was how it worked, not for everyone. When he went out to water the wilting tomato plants, he found Ms. Zhou on her porch fanning herself, and she mentioned that her mother's doctor kept after her about drinking. "Apparently the sense of thirst weakens with age," Ms. Zhou said. "So older people can get dehydrated without ever feeling thirsty. Isn't that something?" Theodore stood there with the hose running over his sneakers and thought about the untouched glass.

That evening he ran a test. He filled a jug, set out eight cups, and told his grandfather it was a new game: every time the chess clock chimed, they both had to empty a cup, no excuses, cheaters forfeit a pistachio from the shared cargo. His grandfather grumbled that forcing water on a man was unfeasible in any civilized country, but he hated losing pistachios more than he hated losing arguments. By bedtime the cups were all empty, and in the morning his grandfather said his headache was gone and he felt like playing a third game of chess, which he also won.

On Friday Theodore taped a chart to the refrigerator, one check mark for every cup. His grandfather studied it, then took the marker and added a column of his own labeled "pistachios fairly distributed," and drew himself a check mark.

"Cheater," Theodore said, and slid the cup across the table.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
The math club room smelled like whiteboard marker and the leftover pizza nobody would claim, and Sebastian had a problem: Mr. Tanaka had written x + 7 = 19 on the board and told everyone to "balance it."

"You can't balance a number," Sebastian said. "It's just sitting there."

"Exactly," said Mr. Tanaka. "It's sitting there like a scale. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other."

Bo leaned over. "So take away seven from both sides. Then the x is alone."

Sebastian wrote x + 7 - 7 = 19 - 7, and underneath it, x = 12. It felt like a magic trick, except magicians never told you how it worked. He tested it, sliding 12 back into the original sentence. Twelve plus seven was nineteen. He checked it twice, because a rule that only worked once wasn't a rule, it was luck.

"Now the bad news," Mr. Tanaka said. "The spring fair is in two weeks. Our booth needs a theme, and the principal wants something about the history of math. One page, printed, by Thursday."

The library after school was desolate, one flickering light and a cart of damaged dictionaries. Sebastian pulled the fattest one down and looked up algebra, mostly because it was the only math word he could spell without thinking. He ran his finger down the column and stopped.

The word came from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. He read it again. The whole subject, every worksheet he'd ever groaned at, had started as part of a book title. He had assumed math was discovered by boring old men in powdered wigs, and it turned out some of it preceded all of that by centuries, sitting in a library in Baghdad while Europe still hadn't invented the fork, probably.

He copied it onto his hand because his notebook was in his locker, which was a decision he would regret.

At the next club meeting, Abbey was guarding the whiteboard like it owed her money. She had written 3x = 24 and was dividing both sides by three, muttering. Sebastian watched her cross out the threes on the left.

"It's like unwrapping something," Abbey said. "You peel off whatever's stuck to the x."

"Peeling," Bo said. "Now my neuron is firing."

"Guess where the word algebra comes from," Sebastian said, before he could lose his nerve.

"Algebrain?" said Bo. "Some Greek guy?"

"Al-jabr. It was part of the title of a book, written around 820 CE in Baghdad. By al-Khwarizmi. A Persian mathematician."

Abbey lowered her marker. "Our entire subject is a leftover book title?"

"It's a good book title," Sebastian said.

Mr. Tanaka looked up from his crossword. "The booth theme is due Thursday."

Sebastian uncapped a fresh marker and wrote across the top of the whiteboard, in letters tall enough to read from the hallway: AL-JABR, EST. 820.

"Nobody will know what it means," Abbey said.

"That's the whole point," said Sebastian. "They'll have to come ask."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
The plush axolotls had cost twelve dollars last month. Now the sign at the mall kiosk said twenty-eight, and a line of kids snaked past the pretzel stand. Keira stared at the bin, which held exactly three axolotls the color of lichen on a wet rock, and did the math in her head. Same toy, same kiosk, more than double the price.

"It's the buyers' fault," said Kayla, holding her phone up with a video of some singer holding the same plush. "Everyone wants one now, so of course it's expensive." Khloe shook her head. "No way. The store just got greedy. Sellers pick whatever price they want, and we have to pay it." They had been arguing since the food court, and Keira had been quiet, because something about the argument bothered her. When the toy sat unwanted in a pile last month, the price had been low. Now the shoppers were migrating toward the kiosk like geese, and the price had climbed with them. It didn't look like only one side was in charge.

"I'll be right back," she said, and walked to the bookstore two doors down. Mr. Augustin was stacking a shelf of economics paperbacks near the window.

"Do you have anything about prices?" she asked. He pointed at a fat old book with a cracked spine, and she flipped it open right there in the aisle. The book was called Principles of Economics, written in 1890 by a man named Alfred Marshall. One line stopped her: he compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors, and said it takes both to set a price.

She carried it back to the kiosk and held it up between her two friends like a referee. "You're both right. This guy Marshall says supply and demand are like the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price." Kayla squinted. "So the buyers pull one blade and the sellers pull the other?" Keira nodded. Khloe looked at the twenty-eight-dollar sign, then at the shrinking bin.

"Then watch this," Khloe said. She marched to the kiosk counter and asked the cashier how many axolotls were left in the back. "None," the cashier admitted. "But we ordered sixty more for Friday." Khloe turned to the line of kids and shouted, "There'll be sixty more on Friday!" Three kids walked away immediately, and one boy put his axolotl back in the bin. Keira grinned and wrote the date on her hand in pen. Friday, they would find out which blade did the cutting.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Before fitting a new tube, the inside of the tyre should be checked for the thorn or glass that caused the flat, or it will puncture again.
story:
Natalie laid the punctured tube on the kitchen table and frowned at it. Two mornings ago she had patched a flat on her bike, pumped the tyre hard, and ridden to school feeling proud. By last period the tyre had gone soft again, and she had wheeled the bike home in the drizzle, listening to Bradley complain that his shoes were soaked.

"You said you fixed it," Bradley said now, perched on a stool with a rubber-band plane in his hands. He wound the propeller and let the plane skitter off the counter and into the fruit bowl.

"I did fix it." Natalie picked up one of the tyre levers Mr. Charles had lent her, a flat plastic wedge the colour of a lemon. "That's the strange part."

Mr. Charles, who lived three doors down, had shown her the basics in his driveway: lever the tyre off the rim, pull out the old tube, work the new one in, pump it up. He had made her do every step herself while he drank his tea. She remembered being impatient with that. She had wanted him to just demonstrate the whole thing so she could watch.

She studied the tube in her hands. A patch on one side, and now a second limp spot near the valve. Two punctures, in different places, two days apart. She turned that over while the kettle ticked behind her. If her patch had failed, the second flat would be in the same spot as the first. It wasn't. So something else was making holes.

Natalie pulled the tyre off the rim, levers squeaking, and spread it open on the table like a stubborn mouth. She ran two fingertips slowly around the inside, pressing lightly, the way she checked apples for bruises at the market. Halfway round, her finger stopped. Something sharp and tiny hid in the rubber, so small she could not see it until she bent close: a sliver of glass, stubborn as a splinter.

"There," she said, and dug it out with a fingernail.

"Is that what got you both times?" Bradley leaned over, plane forgotten.

"Both times. It sat there waiting." Natalie held the sliver up to the window light. She thought about skipping this part again tomorrow, when she was in a hurry, and decided she wouldn't. Some things you check even when you can't see them.

She dusted the tyre's insides with talc, tucked the new tube in place, and clamped the pump head onto the valve. The tyre stiffened under her hands with each stroke.

"That's better," she said, and screwed the cap on tight.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
Mr. Kelly set the timer for twenty minutes, which was exactly how long they had before the math club van left for the county competition. "Equations on the board," he said. "Whatever you can balance before the buzzer, you bring."

Lily copied the first one into her notebook: x + 1 = x + 2. She did what she had taught herself last week, the thing that finally made equations feel fair instead of like magic tricks. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. She subtracted one from both sides and got x = x + 1. She subtracted x from both sides and got 0 = 1.

She stared at that. Down the table, Lauriane was calmly subtracting from both sides of her own problem, and Evelynn was dividing both sides by three, both of them moving steadily toward a number. The room smelled like the orange juice someone had spilled near the puzzle box, and the boy at the far desk was muttering at his paper.

She leaned over. "What have you got?"

The boy, a sixth grader whose name she never remembered, turned his notebook toward her. Same equation. His page was covered with attempts: he had tried 5, and 100, and 0, and even 2.5, which made no sense but he was desperate. "Every number I plug in makes it wrong," he said. "I've been at it since the start and I can't find the number."

Lily tapped her own page, where 0 = 1 sat in pencil. "I don't think the number exists. Look. If x plus one equals x plus two, then the same number would have to be one more and two more than itself at the same time. No number can do that. It just isn't possible."

The boy blinked at her, then at his page of failures, then at her page, which had taken four lines instead of four hundred. "So I wasn't bad at it. There was nothing to find."

"There was nothing to find," Lily agreed. "Some equations have no solution. That one's one of them."

Mr. Kelly drifted past, sipping from a thermos of what he claimed was nectar from the gods and what everyone knew was apple juice. He glanced at the boy's exhausted page and Lily's four lines, and raised an eyebrow at her. "You two mediated a settlement, I see. Both sides got equal treatment."

"Both sides always should," said Lily, and wrote NO SOLUTION in neat capitals.

The buzzer went off. Lauriane and Evelynn collected their papers, the boy closed his notebook with the air of a person retiring from a long war, and Lily was first in line at the door, page held up like proof.

Mr. Kelly checked her answer against his sheet. "Consistent with mine," he said, and waved her onto the van.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: The Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today, was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.
story:
Evan slid the giant climate atlas across the library table so fast that it bumped the pencil cup. He was supposed to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs, and the due date was Friday, and he had exactly one free afternoon. "Ryder, look at this," he said, flipping pages. "Every region has these little letter codes. The rainforest says Af and the desert says BWh."

Ryder didn't look. He was busy stacking his robot club binder, a shoebox of wires, and a bag of pretzels on the far end of the table, because the robot course had to be built tonight and his kitchen table was "a disaster zone." He wanted the big table, the whole thing, and he wanted it now.

"Five minutes," Evan said. "I just need to figure out what Af means. It's like a secret language." He traced the letters with his finger, then noticed a thin line of small print at the bottom of the map. Koppen. Just the one word. He raised his hand and waved until the librarian, Mr. Eze, wandered over from the return cart.

"The map says Koppen," Evan said. "Is that a place?"

Mr. Eze smiled, pulled a climate encyclopedia off the shelf behind him, set it down, and walked away without another word. Evan found the entry himself. Wladimir Koppen. A climatologist. Born in Russia, worked in Germany. He invented the whole classification system, and it was still used on climate maps today. Evan read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it was strange and excellent that the letters on his homework were invented by one actual person.

"Ryder! Some guy named Koppen made up these codes. Born in Russia, worked in Germany, and they still use his system. I bet his descendants see climate maps and point and say, that was our guy." Ryder still didn't answer, so Evan looked up. Ryder had pulled the atlas toward his side of the table. He was drawing a desert sector for the robot course on a sheet laid right over the rainfall graph of the Sonoran.

"That's my graph," Evan said.

"I need a desert for the robot terrain. You need a desert for the homework. Same desert."

"You're covering the numbers. I need the numbers, that's the entire assignment." Evan reached for the atlas. Ryder slid it back. The pencil cup went over, and two people at the next table shushed them.

Before it could get louder, Viola appeared with her stack of books and planted herself in the middle chair. "Okay, I'm mediating. Ryder, you want the atlas for one drawing. Evan, you need the rainfall and temperature numbers for two graphs. Evan, what if you copy your numbers first? Then the atlas is all his." She tapped the empty half of the table. "Split it down the middle, like a treaty."

Evan grabbed a ruler and a fresh sheet and started copying. Twenty centimeters of rain a year in the desert, more than two hundred in the rainforest, a temperature line that stayed flat and warm in one place and swung wildly in the other. Two different worlds, and one alphabet to tell them apart. He wrote Af at the top of his rainforest column and BWh at the top of his desert column, and underlined both.

"Done," he announced, shoving the atlas across the table. Ryder spread out his terrain sketch, then paused. "Wait. Koppen's the letters guy? Then my desert sector is BWh too." He lettered it carefully in the corner. Evan leaned over, held up his copied sheet beside Ryder's drawing, and said, "Same code, two projects. Viola, get the librarian, we're telling him his maps have fans."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
Elijah had been waiting all week for Abby's birthday party, mostly for the basketball hoop in her driveway, but also because Eliane said there would be a chocolate cake with three layers. He arrived with his gift bag swinging, ready for the best Saturday of the month.

Then he heard it in the kitchen. Two boys from his class had cornered a kid named Danny near the snack table, laughing at his dinosaur shirt and the way he counted chips before eating them, one, two, three, like a scientist measuring everything. Danny's ears went pink. The boys got louder because people were watching, and more kids drifted over to see what was funny.

Elijah's first idea was to yell at them, but last month at school he had tried exactly that, and it had exploded into a shoving match that got everyone sent to Ms. Esposito's room. He stood there chewing the inside of his cheek, watching. It struck him that the boys kept glancing around at their audience after every joke, like performers checking for applause. The laughing crowd was doing something, he thought. It was feeding them.

So he tested a different idea. He walked over to Danny, put a hand on his shoulder, and said, "Come on, let's go, I need help carrying the snacks to the basement." Danny blinked, then grabbed a bag of pretzels and followed him down the stairs. The two boys looked at each other. A couple of kids wandered off toward the music. With no audience left, the jokes just sort of ran out of air, like a tire going flat, and the boys shuffled away to find something else to do.

Downstairs, Danny arranged the pretzels in neat rows and even managed a smile. "You nominated me for snack duty," he said. "Nobody's ever nominated me for anything."

"You're the most diligent snack assistant I've ever had," Elijah said, and Danny laughed for real this time.

Upstairs, Ms. Esposito, who lived next door and had come over to drop off a platter, caught Elijah at the punch bowl. "I saw what you did in the kitchen," she said. "That was quick thinking."

"It's my new technique," Elijah said, grinning. "I call it the walk-away plan. I'm going to use it on everybody." Abby stuck her head out of the pantry and shouted that the cake was ready, and Elijah took the stairs two at a time.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
Aiden slid the phone across the lab table like it was made of glass, which, he supposed, it basically was. It had belonged to his cousin, and now it was his, the first phone he had ever owned. "Screen's good," he said, tapping it. "Camera's good." By first period it was at eighty percent. By lunchtime, dead. Again. Third day in a row.

"It's haunted," said Liv, leaning over from the next table. "Or it hates school. Honestly, same." She was building a small hydraulic piston for the robotics showcase, a cardboard cylinder that was supposed to lift a paper claw, and she'd been waiting all week to film it working for her channel. "You're the only person I know with a phone. I need a cameraman Friday. Fix it by then."

Aiden wasn't sure "fix" was the right word, because he wasn't sure anything was broken. On Thursday he tested it. He charged the phone all night, unplugged it at eight, and didn't open a single app. He wrote the percentage on his hand each period like a secret code: eighty at math, sixty at science, thirty by the hallway, dead before the cafeteria finished serving pizza. An app couldn't drain it if he never opened one. So it wasn't the apps. Something inside was the problem.

At the library computer he looked up the battery type and found the word he needed. Then he found more, in a forum where people argued about old phones. He sat very still for a second, then grinned so wide Karam looked up from his book. "It's not haunted. The battery's lithium-ion. When it chemically ages it holds less charge, so battery life just slowly gets shorter." He turned the phone over and popped the back cover. "My cousin charged it every single night for three years. The battery didn't fail. It just got old, like a marathon runner with tiny lungs."

"That is the least spooky haunting ever," Karam said. "Can you replace it?"

"Better," Aiden said. He didn't modify the phone with some wild hack, even though he'd been planning three wild hacks. He ordered a new battery with his allowance, and by Friday afternoon it was in, and the phone sat at seventy-one percent at three o'clock, which felt like a miracle with a number on it.

Liv set her piston on the table, adjusted the claw, and filled the syringe with water. "Ready? Three, two, one." The piston pushed, the claw rose, and it actually, finally worked. Aiden hit record, phone steady in both hands, battery gauge glowing green in the corner. "Say something for your subscribers," he said. Liv looked straight into the lens and said, "Like, subscribe, and trust my cameraman, he knows everything about old batteries."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
Kate had her boots on the dashboard before her dad even started the engine. Reem and Sally piled into the back, still humming the last song from choir practice, and the whole car smelled like wet jackets and winter.

"That was so weird," Sally said, leaning between the front seats. "Devon hit the high note and his voice just snapped in half. Like a squeak, then a croak."

"It's called cracking," Reem said. "My brother does it constantly. He'll say 'pass the bread' and it comes out in two different voices." She demonstrated, dropping low and then leaping up squeaky, and Sally laughed so hard she snorted.

Kate turned around, frowning. "But why? He could hit that note in September. It's like his voice broke something."

"Ms. Sun drew us a picture at the end," Reem said. "There's a thing in your throat called the larynx, and it grows during puberty. The vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker while that happens, and that's when the cracking happens."

Kate sat with that all the way to the first stoplight. Longer and thicker. She hummed a low note to test it, so quiet the others couldn't hear. Her own voice felt steady. But her throat hadn't grown yet, probably, so that didn't eliminate anything. She needed to think it through like a math problem: if the folds were longer, like longer strings on a piano or a longer rubber band, they would sound deeper. That was probably why men had lower voices. And while the growing was still going on, the folds couldn't decide what they were yet, so the sound jumped. It was like a door that stuck halfway before it swung open.

"Okay," she said out loud. "So it isn't that Devon is a bad singer. His throat is literally under construction."

"Right," Reem said. "Ms. Sun said not to laugh at boys when it happens, but honestly it's hard."

Kate glanced at Sally, who had gone quiet, picking at her glove. "What if my voice cracks?" Sally asked. "In the spring concert. In front of everybody."

"Then the same thing is happening to you, that's all," Kate said. "Your larynx is growing. It's a concept you can't see, but it's just a body doing its job." She paused. "Also, I'll stand next to you, and if you crack, I'll crack too. On purpose. Then nobody knows who started it."

Sally grinned. "You'd really do that?"

"I've been practicing my squeak since the parking lot," Kate said, and let one rip, a wobbly yodel that made her dad grip the wheel and say, "Please not in the car."

They pulled up at Sally's house, and Sally climbed out backwards, still humming. But this time, when she tried the high note from practice, her voice held, clean and clear, all the way up and all the way down.

"See you Monday," Kate called through the window, and Sally raised her mitten like a conductor finishing a symphony.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
Grandpa Ray leaned forward in the recliner, waving his mug at the TV where the Packers and the Chiefs stood toe to toe at the line of scrimmage. "I'll tell you, I remember the very first Super Bowl like it was yesterday," he announced. "January 15, 1967. Packers against these same Chiefs. Nobody gave Kansas City a chance."

Joseph, sprawled on the rug between his friends Sahib and Remi, sat up straighter. He'd been handing out chips and coordinating the snack runs so nobody missed a play, but now his radar pinged. Grandpa Ray told amazing stories, but some of them got better every year. Last Thanksgiving he'd claimed to have shaken hands with a famous astronaut, and Mom had later rolled her eyes in the kitchen.

"Grandpa, what was the score?" Joseph asked, keeping his voice casual.

"Thirty-five to ten," Grandpa said without missing a beat. "Packers ran away with it."

Remi pulled out her phone. "No fair looking it up," Sahib said, grabbing for it, but Remi was faster, thumbs flying.

"Wait," she said, blinking at the screen. "He's right. January 15, 1967. Packers over the Chiefs, 35 to 10."

Grandpa Ray settled back with the smug look of a man who had just been vindicated. "You kids think everything before phones is fog," he said. "I was fourteen. I watched it at my cousin's place on a tiny black-and-white set, and my uncle yelled so loud the neighbor banged on the wall."

Joseph studied the old framed photo on the shelf, the symmetrical rows of Grandpa's old football trophies lined up like soldiers, and found himself believing it all the way through. Later, while the adults argued about a penalty call, he slid onto the arm of the recliner. "Grandpa, how come you remember the score from before Mom was even born, but you forgot to pick me up at the library last month?"

Grandpa laughed so hard he nearly spilled his mug. He wiped his eyes, set the chips down where Joseph could reach them without stretching, and pointed at the TV. "Because some things matter enough to keep, kid. Now watch. Fourth quarter coming."

On the screen the receiver broke free, and the whole living room rose at once, shouting, and Grandpa's hand came down on Joseph's shoulder like they were on the same team.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
story:
The neon sign above the diner said EAT, and the E had burned out, so it said AT, which Lily decided was still honest enough. She slid into the booth next to her older brother while their dad ordered pancakes for everyone. Outside the window, the van sat in the parking lot with their camping gear wedged in the back, all of it pointed toward Yosemite, three hours north. They had driven along an estuary for the last twenty minutes, gulls wheeling over the place where the river widened into the sea, and Lily kept thinking about bears.

At the next table sat Mr. Carvalho, their neighbor, who had coincidentally chosen the same diner and the same morning for his own trip up the mountain. "You heading to the valley?" he asked, and when Dad nodded, Mr. Carvalho leaned toward Lily's table. "Last year a ranger fined a whole family because the dad left a tube of toothpaste in his tent. In parks like Yosemite, they count anything with a scent as food. Toothpaste, sunscreen, even your trash. It all goes in the bear locker." He tapped the side of his coffee cup. "Bears don't read labels."

Lily thought about that while she ate her toast. Anything with a scent. That was the hidden part, the rule you couldn't see. A bear couldn't smell a number on a sign or a line in a brochure, but it could smell spearmint through canvas. She started making a list in her head: toothpaste, sunscreen, her cherry lip balm, the empty chip bags still in the van's door pocket. Then she remembered her strawberry shampoo, the small bottle zipped into her duffel, which was packed under the tent bag where she couldn't reach it without unpacking half the van.

She tested the idea out loud. "So if the rule is scent, not food, then the stuff that smells strongest matters most," she said. "Sunscreen is more volatile than, like, a granola bar in a sealed wrapper. The smell carries farther." Her brother rolled his eyes, but Dad didn't. He got up, walked out to the van, and came back holding the strawberry shampoo and the cherry lip balm, one in each hand, like evidence.

"We put these in the locker first," he said. "You do the rest."

At the campsite that evening, Lily checked the locker three times. Toothpaste, in. Sunscreen, in. Trash bag, in, because trash counted too. Her brother mocked her for counting items like a bank teller, but he handed over his deodorant anyway. In the morning, a ranger walked the loop and stopped at their site, because a bear had tipped over a cooler two camps down. The ranger checked their locker, checked the tent, and found nothing.

"Only one thing," the ranger said, crouching by the picnic table. She reached under it and pulled out a scrap of foil, smelling faintly of peanut butter. "This was under the bench all night." Lily stared at it, and then at her brother, who had been on PB and J duty. He went pale. "Told you counting helps," Lily said, and dropped the foil into the trash bag, which she carried, at arm's length, straight to the locker.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
Ryder slid his math worksheet across the table at the community centre, far enough that maybe it would fall off the edge and stop being his problem. "Word problems," he said to Justine. "They should be extinct. Like dinosaurs. Nobody misses them."

Justine didn't look up from her notebook. "You're just saying that because you don't get them." The homework club met in the craft room on Tuesdays, with Ms. Girma at the front table and a coffee machine that wheezed like it was dying. Ryder had agreed to participate only because his mother had signed him up and because Justine would be there.

The worksheet read: A taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre. A ride costs 15 dollars. How far did the taxi go? Ryder wrote nothing for a whole minute. Then he remembered the receipt his grandmother had shown him last week, a crumpled slip from a taxi to her doctor's appointment, and how he'd told her they must have gone twelve kilometres because fifteen minus three is twelve. She'd laughed and patted his hand and not corrected him, which had bugged him for days.

He pulled the paper back toward himself. Twelve felt wrong but he couldn't see why, so he decided to test it the way Justine tested guesses, by plugging them in. If they went twelve kilometres at two dollars per kilometre, that was twenty-four dollars, plus three for getting in the cab, twenty-seven dollars total. On a fifteen dollar ride. Way off. He tried six kilometres: twelve dollars for the distance, plus three to start, fifteen. It fit exactly. So the receipt said six kilometres all along, and his guess of twelve had been double, which meant somewhere in his head he'd skipped the price per kilometre entirely.

"Ms. Girma," he called, before he could talk himself out of it. "Is there a way to write this down so I'm not just guessing numbers?" She came over and he copied what she wrote: 3 + 2k = 15. She said do the same thing to both sides, then walked away to help Noah, who had somehow got pencil led smeared across his entire forehead.

Same thing to both sides. Ryder stared at it, then subtracted three from the left side and, obediently, from the right side too. That left 2k = 12. He didn't know what k was yet, but he knew twelve dollars belonged to the kilometres, and twelve divided by two dollars per kilometre gave six. He wrote k = 6 and drew a small, tired box around it, the fatigue of the whole worksheet suddenly lifting off his shoulders.

"It's six," he announced.

"Six what?" said Noah, still smudged.

"Kilometres. My grandma's taxi ride. I told her it was twelve and she just let me believe it." Ryder grabbed his pencil and started the next problem, a bus this time. "That woman is sneaky."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Annabelle sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a pencil in one hand and half a peanut butter cookie in the other. She was drawing the old stone birdbath in the backyard, the one the sparrows splashed in every morning, because Grandma had promised to frame whatever picture Annabelle made this summer. The problem was that the drawing looked boring. Really boring. The birdbath sat right in the middle of the page like a button on a shirt, and the sparrows were just dots around it.

"You keep staring at it," said Mckenzie, who had biked over because she wanted first pick of Grandma's strawberry patch before the birds got them. "Is it broken?"

"It feels wrong and I can't figure out why." Annabelle scrutinized the page, tilting her head, then holding it at arm's length. "Everything's in the right spot. The birdbath is right where it should be."

"Maybe that's the problem," Mckenzie said, chewing a strawberry she had absolutely not negotiated for yet. Grandma had a rule about the garden, and there had been a long negotiation at the screen door involving a bucket and a pair of gardening gloves before Mckenzie got permission.

Annabelle flipped through her grandmother's old art magazines stacked on the windowsill. In one of them she found a photograph of a lighthouse, and the picture had faint lines drawn over it, a grid, two lines up and down and two across, cutting the image into nine boxes. The lighthouse wasn't in the center square. It sat right along one of the lines, near a crossing point. She flipped further and found a painting done the same way, a mountain whose peak touched the top line instead of hovering in the middle. She counted the lines again. Three rows, three columns.

"It's called the rule of thirds," Annabelle said slowly, testing the words. "You divide the picture into a three-by-three grid, and you put the main subject along those lines, or where they cross."

She grabbed a fresh sheet and, very lightly, drew the grid herself. Two vertical lines, two horizontal ones. Then she placed the birdbath not in the center square but where a vertical line crossed a horizontal one, off to the left, and let the fence run along the bottom horizontal line. She added a sparrow perched on the rim, sitting almost exactly on a crossing point. When she held the new drawing up beside the old one, the difference made her blink. The page seemed to open up, like the birdbath had room to breathe, like your eye could travel somewhere.

"Whoa," said Mckenzie, leaning over her shoulder with strawberry juice on her chin. "Do me next. Can you draw me picking berries, but not in the boring middle?"

Annabelle sharpened her pencil and flipped to a clean page. "Stand by the fence," she said, "and hold the bucket up."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
The library smelled like pencil shavings and old glue, and Sophie had been staring at the same wartime poster for twenty minutes. It showed a crowd of soldiers marching behind one smiling man, with the words EVERYBODY IS DOING THEIR PART stamped in red. Ms. Asante had assigned a project on propaganda posters, and Sophie wanted hers to be the one Ms. Asante actually remembered on Monday. Behind her, Aleksandar was building a tower out of encyclopedias, because his plan was to finish his poster in ten minutes and spend the rest of the period making people laugh.

"Everybody is doing it," Sophie read aloud. "That's the whole trick, isn't it? You feel left out if you don't."

Aleksandar slid a volume on top of his tower. "Works on me every time. Isabelle bought the sneakers the volleyball captain wore, and then I bought them, and now we both have sneakers we can't afford."

Sophie remembered the poster Isabelle had taped inside her locker last fall, a famous actor grinning above the words Join the winning team. Isabelle hadn't joined anything. She'd just liked his face. Sophie hadn't thought about it since, but now the poster on the table and the one in the locker seemed to revolve around the same quiet gear, turning somewhere she couldn't see.

She pulled the chunky library computer toward her and typed a search. There it was, in a scanned magazine from the thirties: a group called the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, founded in the United States in 1937, to teach ordinary people how to recognize propaganda. Sophie sat back so fast her chair squeaked. They had made a whole institute for this. Sixty years before she was born, someone had decided that spotting tricks was worth studying.

She tested it on the poster. The smiling man in front was famous, a movie star. Celebrity testimonial, she wrote. EVERYBODY, in red: loaded words. The marching crowd: bandwagon. Her pencil moved faster than it had all week.

"Look," she said, turning the notebook toward Aleksandar. "Three tricks in one poster. Guess which one gets you."

He studied it, chin in hand, and his tower of encyclopedias wobbled. "Not the crowd part. I'm not biased, I just really wanted those sneakers."

"That's the crowd part," Sophie said.

The tower came down with a crash that echoed off the ceiling. Ms. Asante looked up from the desk, and Aleksandar's reflex was to point at the encyclopedia on top, as if it had started it. Sophie slid her notebook out of the wreckage and kept writing.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A Python for loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without reaching break, which fits 'no divisor found, so the number is prime'.
story:
Parker typed the number 9 into his program and watched the screen say PRIME, which was wrong, and had been wrong all afternoon. The club room smelled like the janitor's floor wax, and Juan kept leaning over his shoulder to watch the same bug happen again, as if it might change its mind. Demo night was in forty minutes, and Ms. Fortin had already promised the principal that three working programs would signify the club's whole semester of work. Parker's program, his prime checker, kept handing out verdicts that made no sense.

The problem was hiding somewhere in his loop. He could see the loop, could see the dividers and the remainders, but he could not see why the program jumped straight to "prime" without ever finding the 3 that divided 9. He tried putting the print statement outside the loop, then inside, then both, and got "not prime" printed nine times, which Juan said looked like the program was having a panic attack. Parker felt that panic was contagious.

Jacob, at the next table, was building a dice roller for demo night and wanted the first slot, the one with the best lighting. He kept glancing over, not to help, but to count how far ahead he was. When Parker groaned for the third time, Jacob wandered over anyway. "My cousin went to a coding camp last summer," he said. "The mentor showed his table a loop trick. Watch this." Jacob reached across the keyboard, typed an else under Parker's for loop, and lined it up with the for instead of the if.

"That's not where else goes," Parker said. "Else belongs to the if."

"Not this one," Jacob said. "The camp guy said it runs only if the loop finished without hitting break."

Parker stared at the two lines. So the loop could march through every possible divisor, break the moment it found one, and if it never broke, if it finished the whole march empty-handed, the else would fire. No divisor found, so the number was prime. The whole thing rearranged itself in his head like tiles sliding into place. He deleted his tangled flag variable, the one he had copied from an old program last month and never really understood, and wrote the loop clean: divide, check, break, else print prime. Last month he had skipped the tricky part and patched over it, a habit his old teacher had once called chronic, and he still wasn't sure he'd broken it, or only covered it again.

He typed 9. NOT PRIME. He typed 7. PRIME. He typed 25, then 2, then 97, and the verdict came back correct every single time. Ms. Fortin stopped behind him, read the screen twice, and said, "Run it once more," so he did, and it held.

At demo night Jacob got the first slot after all, and his dice roller crashed on the number 12. Parker was second. He stood at the projector, typed 9 into his own program in front of everyone, and said, "Last week this thing told me nine was prime." The screen said NOT PRIME. "Ask it anything," he told the room, and Juan, sitting in the front row, called out, "Fifty-one."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact:
Most HTML tags come in pairs: an opening tag like

and a closing tag with a slash,

, wrapped around the content.
story:
Emile stared at the laptop in Fanny's basement, where the ceiling had those little bumpy tiles and a poster of an owl hung crooked over the shelf. He had typed one line into his brand new web page, and now the entire page was one enormous heading. The word "Owls" filled the screen edge to edge, and under it, in letters just as gigantic, was every sentence he had written about owls being nocturnal, and how some owl species are in danger of extinction. It looked like a poster for a monster movie.

"Your page ate itself," said Fanny, peering over his shoulder.

"Pages don't eat themselves," Emile said. "Something I typed did this."

Tommy bounced a tennis ball off the basement wall, caught it, bounced it again. "Maybe the computer is broken. My dad's computer does weird stuff all the time."

"It's not broken." Emile scrolled up to look at his code. He had promised his cousin he would build this page tonight, and the owl club needed a real website by Friday, not a page that looked like it was shouting. He read the line at the top, out loud, slowly. He had typed the opening angle bracket, h1, the closing bracket, then the word Owls. Then more brackets, more text, more brackets. Somewhere in there, he figured, was the difference between a heading and a disaster, but you could not see it by looking at the giant page. The page only showed the result.

He tried an experiment. He deleted a single letter, typed it back, and hit refresh. Nothing changed. The page still roared at him in monster letters. So the problem was not that one letter. He moved his eyes down the code, line by line, like a detective counting suspects. Then he saw it. Near the top, right after the word Owls, he had typed a closing bracket and then nothing else. No slash. He compared it to a later line, where he had typed a bracket, a slash, and then the letter h and the number 1, all wrapped around another word. That line ended something.

"Wait," he said. "Most of these tags come in pairs. You open one, and you close one, with a slash in it. Mine never closed."

"Like a door," Fanny said. "Yours is open, so everything after it walked in."

Tommy stopped bouncing the ball. "So everything on the whole page walked into your heading. That's why it's all giant."

Emile added the slash so the closing tag matched the opening one, saved, and refreshed. The word "Owls" shrank to a proper heading at the top, and the rest of the page turned back into ordinary text. He leaned back and let out a breath.

"Now for the centring," he said. "Ms. Cardinal says a lopsided heading looks like a bad haircut."

Fanny pulled the keyboard toward her. "Then let's verify that the slash stays put." She scrolled up, tapped the screen right on the little angled line, and grinned. "Little slash, big difference."

"Everything on the internet is held together by one punctuation mark," Tommy said, and he bounced the ball off the wall one more time.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In French, à droite means to the right, while tout droit means straight ahead, a pair that often trips up learners asking for directions.
story:
Landon had one week before the class trip to Montréal, and he still could not tell droite from droit. Mr. Zhang had written both on the board, and the whole class was supposed to practice asking for directions until the words stuck.

"Pretend I'm lost," said Luka, spinning a pencil between his fingers. "You ask, I answer, we trade places. And if you get us to the boulangerie, I'll delegate the snack buying to you." Luka's real want was simpler: he wanted first pick of the pastries, and he trusted only someone who could actually find the bakery.

Landon tried it in his head. "Où est la boulangerie, s'il vous plaît?" Then the answer would come, and that was where the trouble started. He turned to Ewan, who was leaning over their handout. "If somebody says tout droit, which way do I go?"

"Straight ahead," Ewan said, without looking up. "Not right. That's the trap."

A memory floated back to Landon then. Last spring, his cousin had come home from a school trip to France with a story about a passer-by giving directions in careful French, and his whole group turning right at the corner when they should have kept walking straight ahead. They had circled the block twice, laughing, before anyone untangled it. At the time Landon had thought it was funny. Now it felt like a warning.

He decided to test the idea instead of just worrying about it. He drew a quick network of streets on the back of his handout, a grid of lines like graph paper, then imagined a route across it. "Okay, Luka. Ask me."

"Où est la boulangerie?"

"Continuez tout droit," Landon answered, and slid his finger straight up the map, past two intersections, not turning at all. Then he tried the other word. "Tournez à droite," he said, and this time his finger bent to the right at the first corner. He did it again and again, left hand pointing, right hand holding the pencil, until the two paths felt different in his muscles, not just in his memory.

Mr. Zhang wandered past their desks and watched the moving finger for a moment. "Pretend the paper is a porous sponge," he said mildly. "Let the streets soak in."

That evening Landon walked the route to his own corner store, mouthing the phrases to himself, straight ahead when he meant tout droit, a turn when he meant à droite. The autumn light came slanting through the porous hedge along his street, laying small bright spots on the sidewalk, and he counted intersections like a map coming alive.

In Montréal, on the second morning, Luka grabbed his sleeve near a fountain. "You're the navigator. Find the bakery." A woman with a canvas bag paused when Landon asked his question, and she gestured up the street: "Tout droit, puis à droite." Landon led them straight past the fountain, then turned right at the corner, and the bakery's warm smell rolled out through the open door. Luka pushed past him to the counter. "Two chocolate ones," he called over his shoulder. "You earned it."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
The letter to the local paper had been taped inside Charlotte's binder since Monday, because it was about the new skate park, and the skate park was the only thing she had argued about at dinner for two weeks. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste," her dad had read out loud, tapping the sentence with his fork. "Half of that you could check," he said, "and half you couldn't." Charlotte had chewed on that, along with her noodles, all the way through the meal.

At lunch on Wednesday she spread the letter on the table between Alisha and Justice. "My dad says this sentence is two things mashed together," she said. "But he wouldn't tell me which half is which, because he thinks I should figure it out myself, which is so unfair."

Justice leaned over it. "Two million dollars. Somebody wrote that down somewhere. Money leaves a trail." Alisha pointed at the end of the sentence. "'A waste' leaves no trail. My brother calls everything a waste. His haircut. His sandwich. The moon."

Charlotte wrote the sentence across the top of her notebook, then drew a line down the middle of the page. "So this side is stuff we could check if we wanted to," she said, printing cost two million dollars on the left, "and this side is stuff that's just how somebody feels." She printed a waste on the right and sat back. "One sentence. Both kinds."

"That's actually creepy," Justice said, peering at it. "It's dressed up like a fact the whole way through."

By Friday Charlotte had a system, and she tested it on everything she could get her hands on. In the cafeteria she picked announcements off the bulletin board and sorted them aloud. "The bake sale raised three hundred twelve dollars, checkable. The gym smells like a wet dog, opinion." The vice principal, walking past with his coffee, gave her a look. She tested it in Ms. Gallagher's class when a boy said the abandoned lot behind the school looked desolate. "Checkable?" Charlotte whispered to Alisha. Alisha shook her head. "You can count chain-link fences, but desolate is a feeling about them." Charlotte added it to the right-hand column, third item down.

When it was her turn to present on Monday, Charlotte stood up with her notebook and articulated her idea in one careful sentence: "A single sentence can mix both, so the checkable part and the opinion part can be hiding inside the same words." She read the park sentence to the class and watched half the hands go up. Justice called out, "Two million is checkable, the rest is someone's perspective," and Ms. Gallagher wrote the sentence on the board and drew a line straight down the middle of it.

After class Alisha caught her at the door. "So for the town meeting, are we going to check the number or argue about the waste part?"

"Both," Charlotte said. "But first I'm calling the parks office. Ask them if they count fence posts."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Ryan had always thought that growing up would announce itself in some obvious way, like a voice cracking in front of the whole class or a sudden mustache. Instead it had announced itself at the shoe store. Twice in one school year, his shoes had stopped fitting, and the second time his mother marched him to the pharmacy to use the foot-measuring slide next to the aisle of insoles, because the shoe store clerk had looked at her like she was exaggerating.

"Now that's strange," his mother said, watching the metal slider glide past the line where his toe used to sit. "Size eight and a half. In September you were a seven." She held up the measuring device as if it might be broken. Ryan looked down at his jeans, which still fit fine, and then at his feet, which looked, in his opinion, like they belonged to somebody else. His mom went off toward the vitamin shelf, leaving him alone with the measuring slide and a theory forming in his head.

The pharmacy was a good place to test a theory, he decided, because nobody paid attention to a kid messing with a foot measurer. He slipped off one shoe and pressed his hand flat against his palm print on the cold metal, comparing. His hands looked longer too. He was still evaluating that evidence when Kaylin from his science class appeared at the end of the aisle, holding a box of bandages and staring.

"Are you measuring your hand with the foot thing?" she asked.

"I'm testing something," Ryan said. "My feet went up a size and a half since September, but my jeans still fit, and my hands look bigger. So I think feet and hands grow first, before the rest of you catches up."

Kaylin squinted at her own sneakers, then at his. "That would explain why Marcus trips over nothing in gym," she said slowly, like she was running the idea against every tall, clumsy kid she knew. "His feet are enormous and he's still short." She paused. "Of course, it could be neutral. It could just be you and Marcus."

"It's a decent candidate for a rule, though," Ryan said. "I'm going to measure my hand every month and see if my arms figure out what's going on eventually."

His mother came back with the vitamins, glanced at the slide, and sighed at the price of size eight and a half shoes. Kaylin paid for her bandages and, on her way out, pointed at Ryan's feet and mouthed, "Keep me posted."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
Mason stared at the page of homework in front of him and felt like the numbers were mocking him. x + 7 = 15. He knew x had to be 8, but only because he'd counted on his fingers under the table, and Mr. Tan had made it very clear that guessing was not a method. "Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other," Mr. Tan had said, and Mason had written it down, and now it sat at the top of his page like a rule that refused to explain itself. Why both sides? Who decided that?

He tipped his chair back, which his mom always said would end badly, and glared at the equals sign itself. Two short parallel lines, sitting there like train tracks going nowhere. Had someone just made that up? Somebody must have drawn the very first one, the way somebody drew the first question mark or the first plus sign. Mason sat forward so fast the chair legs banged the floor. He pulled his dad's ancient math encyclopedia off the shelf above the toaster, the one with the cracked spine that fell open to whatever page it felt like.

The page it fell open to was not about equations at all. It was about symbols. Mason ran his finger down the column, past plus and minus and that weird long division bracket, and then stopped. There it was: the equals sign had been invented by a Welsh mathematician named Robert Recorde in 1557. And when Recorde chose the symbol, he had picked two parallel lines because, as the book quoted him, no two things could be more equal. Mason read the line twice, then a third time, and a slow grin spread across his face. The sign wasn't random. It was an argument. Two lines, perfectly matched, exactly the same length, exactly the same slant. The symbol itself was saying, these two sides are the same.

"So that's why you can't just do stuff to one side," he said out loud to the empty kitchen. If both sides were truly equal, like twin parallel lines, then whatever operation hit the left one had to hit the right one too, or the lines wouldn't match anymore. It was like a signal, and until now he'd been ignoring it. He tried x + 7 = 15 and subtracted 7 from both sides. x = 8. Then he got aggressive and made up a harder one, 3x = 21, and divided both sides by 3. x = 7. He checked it. It worked. He checked it again. It still worked.

Just then his phone buzzed. It was a text from Rachael: "stuck on homework, mr tan's problems are evil, did you figure out the both sides thing?" Mason typed back, "come over. I know who invented the equals sign and it will change your life." There was a long pause, then: "that is the least cool sentence anyone has ever texted me. omw."

While he waited, Mason tried to restrict himself to the assigned problems, but he couldn't help making up a monster equation for Rachael: x + 7 = 15, then 3x = 21, then one with fractions, all stacked on the page. He drew two neat parallel lines at the top and wrote underneath, in his most careful handwriting, "no two things could be more equal." When the doorbell rang, he slid the paper across the table toward the empty chair beside him.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A "parking lot" is a list where a meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item.
story:
Quinn pushed the kitchen table against the window so there was room for six chairs, then set her notebook at the head like a tiny podium. The Garden Club had met three times already, and every time the same thing happened: fifteen minutes on tomatoes, then an hour of everybody talking at once. Today she had written an agenda on the back of a cereal box, with times next to each item, and she had practiced saying "next item" to the bathroom mirror until her little brother asked if she was okay.

Zion arrived first, carrying a lush basil plant he had grown from seed, its leaves fat and glossy. He set it in the center of the table like it was the guest of honor. "I want the first agenda item to be the balcony project," he said. "Laila and I already measured my balcony. Four containers. We could grow herbs up there by June."

"Herbs are item three," Quinn said, tapping the cereal box. "Item one is the school courtyard cleanup."

Laila arrived with Ms. Nakamura, their neighbor, who had offered her spare trowels and stayed to watch, mug of tea in hand. Quinn took a breath and began. "Item one, the cleanup. We need to decide the date."

"June would be perfect for the balcony," Zion said. "Also, I've been thinking, we could sell the herbs at the spring fair and donate the money. There's that fundraising idea, and once we had money we could buy a rain barrel, which connects to water conservation, which could be a whole workshop..."

Quinn watched the clock. Three minutes gone, and they were somewhere in the rain-barrel region of nowhere. Last week she had tried talking louder, and it had not worked, and afterwards she had sat on the stairs trying to figure out why. Loudness was not the problem, she realized. The problem was that Zion's ideas were good, so nobody wanted to shut them down, and there was nowhere to put them. An idea with nowhere to go just circles the room like a fly.

She held up her hand, palm out, and Zion stopped mid-sentence. "I just remembered something," she said. "My mom runs meetings at work, and she keeps a parking lot."

"A what?" Laila asked.

"A parking lot. It's a list where the meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item."

Zion frowned. "So my ideas get parked?"

"Your ideas get saved," Quinn said. "Nothing gets thrown away." She turned to a fresh page, wrote PARKING LOT at the top, and under it: "Zion: herb sale at spring fair, money for rain barrel." She looked up. "Item one. The cleanup. Date?"

"Saturday the fourteenth," Laila said, and Zion nodded, because his idea was sitting right there on the page where he could see it.

They finished three agenda items in twenty minutes.
