Quinn could speculate all she wanted about why it worked, but watching Zion glance at the parking lot page twice, checking that his basil sale was still there, she thought she already knew. When they reached the end of the agenda, she said, "Now the parking lot. Zion, tell us about the spring fair."

Zion stood up so fast his chair scraped the floor. "Okay, so," he said, "imagine a table, right, and it's covered in little pots of basil."

Ms. Nakamura raised her mug. "I'll take two," she said.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
Oliver had forty dollars of birthday money in his pocket, and the tablet kiosk in the middle of the mall was calling his name. The screen above the counter flashed five huge bullet points: FASTEST PROCESSOR, CRYSTAL CLEAR SCREEN, THOUSANDS OF APPS, ULTRA LIGHT, LOVED BY MILLIONS. A video played on loop showing a famous singer holding the tablet and saying, "I never leave home without mine." Behind him, a wall of photos showed crowds of smiling customers, and a banner read, "The amazing tablet everyone is buying."

Ajay and Roxane had come along to keep him honest, though so far they were mostly being no help. "The singer has one," Ajay said, staring up at the screen. "And millions of people bought it. It must be good."

"That's the point," Roxane said. "They want you to think that. Mr. Lim told us ads do that. He called one of them a celebrity testimonial."

Oliver pulled out the phone his mom made him carry and searched the tablet's name. Every review mentioned five things, the same five on the poster. But he noticed something odd. He checked a second review site, then a third, typing in the words "problems" and "battery." There it was. On a forum, user after user said the battery lasted barely three hours, and when Oliver found a photo of the box in small print, it listed the battery specs that the ad never once mentioned.

"They're stacking the deck," he said slowly. "It's called card stacking. Showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it. That's why the ad seems stronger than it is."

"So it's not a lie," Ajay said, frowning at the poster. "Fastest processor is probably true."

"It's true," Oliver said, "but it's not the whole truth." He had been one tap away from handing over his forty dollars as a deposit. He turned to the counter and asked the cashier, "What's the battery life on this?" The cashier paused just long enough for all three of them to notice, then said two and a half hours, maybe more if the screen was dim.

Ajay changed his mind right there. "Okay, I wanted one because everyone has one. That was dumb."

"It wasn't dumb," Roxane said. "You checked before you bought it. That's the whole trick."

On the way to the food court, they made it systematic, walking past store windows and calling out the tricks they spotted: the sneaker ad with a basketball star, the energy drink poster shouting "the greatest taste ever." They even mediated a small argument about whether "greatest" counted as a loaded word, and settled it by looking up what loaded meant. By the time they reached the climax of the afternoon, the soft pretzel stand, Oliver still had his forty dollars.

"Next weekend," he said, "we research first, then buy." He held up his phone and snapped a picture of the pretzel stand's sign, which claimed the best pretzels in the universe. "Starting with this."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Lincoln stood in his grandfather's hallway with the reading for his coming-of-age ceremony folded in his back pocket. In two weeks he had to recite all fourteen lines from memory, in front of both sides of the family, and so far he could manage four. He had read the lines aloud maybe fifty times in his bedroom, and each time they seemed to slide back out of his head the moment he closed the page.

"I'm pessimistic about this," he told Jet, who had biked over to keep him company. "I'm going to stand up there and say the second half first."

Jet was looking at the photographs on the wall. "Your grandpa's house is huge. How many rooms is this?"

"Eight, plus the sun porch." Lincoln followed his gaze down the hallway. The kitchen at the front, the living room, the dining room, the study, the two bedrooms, the bathroom, the porch. Rooms he had walked through since he was four years old.

He unfolded the paper and read the first line again. Something about beginning. He walked into the kitchen and set the line there in his mind, on the counter next to the cookie jar, the way you might set down a set of keys. Then he walked to the living room and placed the second line on the mantel under the clock. Third line went on the dining room table. Fourth line, the study desk. He kept going, room by room, until the last line sat on the porch rail beside the watering can.

Then he walked back to the front door, closed his eyes, and moved through the house in his mind. Kitchen, cookie jar, first line. Mantel, clock, second line. It worked. The lines came out in order, the way houses come in order when you walk through them.

Lauriane arrived just then with her grandmother's recipe cards, and Lincoln explained what he had done. "My mom calls it the method of loci," she said. "She memorizes her speeches that way."

"By putting the words in places?"

"Along a route you already know. Then you walk the route in your head and the words are waiting there."

Lincoln grinned. He tried it again, start to finish, with Jet timing him on his phone. Forty seconds, no mistakes. When Jet asked what he would do if he got nervous and his mind went blank at the ceremony, Lincoln said he had a plan for that too. "Panic is like an invading army. It only takes territory nobody's guarding. Every line in that house has a guard on it."

"That's a metaphor," Jet said.

"It's the truth," Lincoln said, and walked the hallway again, touching each doorframe as he passed.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
The bus rattled toward the county bee, and Rebecca flipped through her word list for the hundredth time. Across the aisle, Carmelo was bouncing his knee so hard the seat shook. "I just want to beat Mikayla," he said. "She beat me in the geography fair, the science fair, and the rock-paper-scissors semifinal. This is my year."

"Your year, and also the year of the fourteen other candidates on this bus," Rebecca said, nodding at the seats full of spellers from other schools. One boy was whispering words to himself like a haunted calculator.

Mikayla leaned over the back of her seat. "Quiz me. Go." Rebecca read, "Insulate." Mikayla spelled it perfectly, then added, "It means to cover something so heat or electricity can't get through, like the foam in this bus's walls, which are clearly failing, because I'm freezing."

Rebecca laughed, but inside she felt the old knot tighten. Last year she had gone out on "saguaro," and she hadn't even tried to figure it out. She had just stood there, guessed a couple of vowels, and walked off the stage. Later, lying awake in her arid, air-conditioned bedroom, she had replayed it and realized she'd given up without using any of her options. She'd heard other spellers ask questions at the microphone, but she'd never paid attention to what was allowed.

"Ms. Halvorsen," she called to the teacher up front, "at the real Scripps bee, what are spellers allowed to ask for?"

Ms. Halvorsen turned around. "You may ask for the definition, the part of speech, the language of origin, or a sentence using the word. The judges have to answer." She smiled. "County bees follow the same rules."

Rebecca's heart sped up. A definition. A sentence. Language of origin. She remembered the kid who had spelled "schtum" last year only after asking where it came from, and it suddenly made sense: German words had German patterns. If she knew a word came from Spanish, she'd know there was no silent k. It was like being handed a map right before walking into a maze.

"Ask me one," she told Mikayla. "Something impossible."

"Bougainvillea."

Rebecca closed her eyes. "May I have the language of origin?" she asked, playing both parts. "French, from a botanist's name," she answered herself, "so it's probably spelled the French way, with all those letters sitting together like passengers on a crowded bus." She spelled it out, letter by letter, and Mikayla shrieked, "Correct!"

Carmelo groaned. "Great. Now I have to beat both of you."

The bus groaned too, downshifted, and pulled into the parking lot behind the auditorium. Rebecca zipped her word list into her backpack and stood first in the aisle, fingers already curled around an invisible microphone.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
story:
Zoey sat at the kitchen table with her German notebook open and a pencil that had already lost its eraser. Her assignment was to describe her family and her pets in full sentences, and so far she had written one sentence about her dog, Biscuit, and then crossed it out because she was not sure if Biscuit was masculine or feminine in German. Down the hall she could hear her three little brothers racing toy cars, and her sister was singing the same four lines of a song over and over. The house was not a quiet place for homework.

She tried again. "Ich habe einen Hund," she wrote, and then came the hard part. "Ich habe drei Brüder und eine Schwester." She counted the words and frowned. In English she could just say "four siblings," which was short and done. In German she seemed stuck spelling it all out, and if she had to read her paragraph out loud in Mr. Petrov's class tomorrow, she would be standing there forever while Kyson and Dave smirked from the second row.

Then she remembered something. Last week Mr. Petrov had said a word on the board and moved on quickly, and she had copied it without knowing why. She flipped back two pages. There it was: Geschwister. She squinted at it, then tested a simple idea. She texted Dave, who was also in the class and annoyingly good at vocabulary. "Does Geschwister mean brothers and sisters together? Like one word for all of them, the way English uses siblings?"

"Ya," Dave texted back. "Geschwister. You didn't know that?"

Zoey grinned and wrote her new sentence: "Ich habe vier Geschwister." Two words instead of five, and it even covered her sister without a separate sentence. It was a small insight, but it felt like finding a shortcut through a hedge. She kept going, describing her mother as helpful, her father as tall, and Biscuit as loud, which was generous to Biscuit.

Her brother Theo wandered into the kitchen holding a broken toy car. "Can you fix it?" he asked. Zoey was tempted to say no and be pessimistic about it, since the wheel had vanished somewhere under the couch and was probably gone forever. Instead she said, "Delegate. You find the wheel, I'll fix the axle." Theo dropped to the floor and searched, and when he held up the wheel triumphantly, she snapped it back on for him. He hugged her leg and ran off, and she went back to her paragraph feeling like the whole evening had gone two words shorter than expected. She read her last sentence out loud to the empty kitchen, and Biscuit barked in agreement.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Hazel dumped the duffel bag onto the table in the school's family-studies room and stared at the mountain of clothes Mr. Kapoor had left for the laundry unit. Her partner, Liam, pulled out his hockey jersey first and held it up like a trophy. "This has to be perfect by Friday," he said. "Coach says if we look sloppy, we play sloppy."

"Then let's not turn it pink," Hazel said. She began sorting, whites in one pile, darks in another, colours in a third. A red sock lurked near the bottom, and she fished it out before it could orbit its way into the whites and ruin everything.

Liam's stack included a white shirt with blue stripes, and next to it a truly grey practice shirt. "These need bleach," he said, reaching for the bottle on the shelf. "The striped one's gone dull."

Hazel caught his wrist. Something was nagging at her. The striped shirt was new, and she'd seen tiny printed symbols stitched into the seam. She turned the shirt inside out and found the care label, a little strip of writing with a row of small icons. There was a tub, an iron, and a triangle with a cross through it. The grey practice shirt's label showed a plain, empty triangle instead.

"That's a contradiction," Hazel said slowly. "Same kind of shirt, same fabric almost, but the symbols don't match." She held the two labels side by side. "The empty one has to mean it's okay, and the crossed-out one has to mean no. It means it must not be bleached."

"Then what do we do about my striped shirt?" Liam asked, deflating a little.

"Hot water and detergent, and a good long soak," Hazel said. "No bleach. If it doesn't work, you wear it dull." Liam opened his mouth to argue, then looked at the crossed-out triangle again and closed it. "Fine," he said. "But the jersey gets the full treatment."

They loaded the machine, measured the detergent, and started the wash with only the grey shirt and a few true whites in the bleach load. While it churned, they folded towels from the finished load, and Hazel found that vigorous shaking before folding made the towels lie flat instead of bunching into lumps.

When the cycle ended, Liam held up the grey shirt, bright and clean, and then his striped one, soaked and hung to dry, its blue stripes still exactly blue. He grinned. "Dull stripes, alive colours. I can live with that." Hazel slid the bleach bottle back onto the shelf, label out, so the next person would know to check the triangle first.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
story:
The baby monitor crackled at 10:58, three minutes after Grayson had settled onto the couch with his homework. He listened. A thin, rising wail came through the speaker, the kind that would not stop on its own. Ms. Kobayashi had left him a list on the fridge, written in tidy blue ink, and next to the words "diaper change" she had added a note in the margin: "Wash hands after, before food. Twenty seconds. Sing the chorus twice." He had read it twice earlier, wondering why she bothered to write something so obvious, but the wail got louder, so he carried little Ben up to the changing table and got to work.

It was worse than he had pictured. When it was over, he stood there holding his breath, arms damp, and considered his options. He could rinse quickly under the tap and get to the bottle warming on the counter. Or he could follow the note exactly, soap and all, through a whole twenty seconds of scrubbing before he prepared Ben's lunch. He looked at his hands under the hallway light. They looked clean. But looks, he thought, were exactly the problem. Whatever was on them, if anything, was too small to see, which meant he could not judge by looking. That was the part that interested him, in a restless, uncomfortable way.

So he tested it. At the kitchen sink, he pumped soap onto his palms, turned on the water, and hummed the chorus of the song stuck in his head, once, then twice, checking the clock above the stove. Two choruses came out to just past twenty seconds. He kept scrubbing the whole time, between his fingers, around his thumbs, backs of his hands, then rinsed and dried them on the clean towel before he touched the bottle.

Ben ate sweet potato with his fists and thrived on it, smearing orange across the high chair tray and grinning like he had discovered something wonderful. Grayson found himself grinning back. "You're a mess," he said, "but at least I did the math on my hands before your lunch." Ben banged the tray in reply.

At noon the door opened, and Ms. Kobayashi came in shaking rain off her coat. "How did it go?" she asked. "The diaper, I mean. First-timers usually look shaken."

"It went fine," Grayson said. "But why twenty seconds exactly? And why the chorus twice?"

She smiled as she lifted Ben out of the chair. "Twenty seconds of scrubbing is what health agencies recommend, after a diaper change and before preparing food. The chorus just fills the time." She shrugged. "Sing anything you like."

Grayson nodded slowly, filing that away. Then he pointed at the counter. "There's still half a jar left, and I already washed. Want me to warm it while you take off your boots?"

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Charles sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table with his left arm propped on a pillow, the cast already itching in three places he couldn't reach. Taylor sat on the plastic chair by the window, turning the fact over out loud, because that was what Taylor did. "The doctor said it's only partly broken. How can a bone be partly broken?"

"A greenstick fracture," Charles said, using the words the doctor had written on the paper in his file. "That's what it's called."

"But what does it mean?" Taylor leaned forward. "Greenstick. Like a stick that's green?"

Charles had been wondering the same thing since Monday. The doctor had said the bone cracked on one side and bent on the other, and that it happened mostly in kids because their bones were more flexible, like a young green branch. That part stuck in his head and wouldn't let go. Cracked on one side, bent on the other. Which side cracked? The outside of the bend, or the inside?

"Think about it," Charles said. "When you bend something, one side gets stretched and the other side gets squished." He held up his good hand and curved it like a bow. "So which side breaks first?"

"The squished side?" Taylor guessed.

"That's what I thought. But wait." Charles looked around the room. On the counter sat a box of wooden tongue depressors, and next to it a clipboard the receptionist had asked his mom to authorize, signing the forms for the follow-up visit. Charles reached with his right hand and took one wooden stick. "Don't tell," he said, and bent it slowly, watching both sides the way you watch a kettle before it boils. The outside of the curve went pale and split into tiny lines. The inside just compressed. When he bent further, the outside snapped through while the inside stayed connected, bent.

"The stretched side," he said. "The outside of the bend cracks, and the inside just bends. Green stick. Because a dry old stick snaps clean through both sides."

Taylor took a fresh depressor and tried it, and then a third, in vain, trying to get one to break on the inside of the curve instead. Every single one cracked on the outside first. "So your bone did this," Taylor said, holding up the split-but-hinged stick, "on your arm."

"And it happens to kids mostly, not grown-ups, because our bones are still bendy." Charles turned his cast arm over, imagining the hidden line inside it, one side cracked, one side bent, mending in there where he couldn't see. He wondered whether the two sides healed at different speeds. He decided he would ask.

The door opened and Mr. Tremblay from next door poked his head in, there for his own appointment, holding his hat. "Still in one piece, Charles?"

"Mostly," Charles said, and held up the bent tongue depressor. "Want to see a picture of my arm?"

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
story:
Bentley slid his new glasses on in the back of Ms. Clarke-Williams's classroom, and the whole room sharpened at once. He could read the tiny copyright line on the poster by the window. He could count the tiles in the ceiling. He could see that Aryan had drawn a tiny rocket on the corner of his homework.

"Let me try," said Youssef, and Bentley handed them over, though his instinct said no, not my new glasses. Youssef squinted, blinked, and handed them back fast. "The floor is way too close."

Bentley thought about Saturday. He remembered the optometrist's office, the chair that leaned back, the row of letters shrinking line by line until they looked like ants. His dad had mentioned that Bentley spent all weekend indoors, every weekend, on screens. The optometrist had nodded and said, "Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood." Bentley had filed that away. Now he turned it over. Was that why his eyes went wrong, all those weekends of screens and no sky? There was no way to see it directly. He would have to test it.

At recess he found Aryan and Youssef on the blacktop. "Question," Bentley said. "Who here has glasses?" Aryan raised his hand. Youssef shook his head. "And who spends weekends outside?" Youssef pointed at himself. Aryan shrugged. "Xbox," he said. "Basically dawn to dinner." Bentley grinned so wide the glasses slid down his nose. Two kids was a small sample, sparse evidence, but the pattern held, and he wanted more of it. He made a chart in his notebook that afternoon: every kid in class, glasses or no glasses, indoors or outdoors. He knew the survey would have to precede any real conclusion, so he asked everyone the same two questions and kept careful tally marks.

By Friday the pattern was still holding, more or less, and Bentley had decided that weekend number one of the new outdoor life would start immediately. Then came the twist. Ms. Clarke-Williams stopped by his desk, looked at his chart, and laughed. "Interesting project, Bentley. I've worn glasses since I was eight." He checked his column for her, and there it was, written in his own neat pencil: Ms. Clarke-Williams, no glasses.

"You have contacts," Bentley said.

"I do. And I grew up on a farm. Outside all day, every day, and I still ended up nearsighted." She tapped his chart. "So your pattern has a hole in it."

Bentley stared at the tally marks. So being outdoors made nearsightedness less common, but it was no guarantee, more like a coin that landed heads more often than tails. He drew a small arrow from Ms. Clarke-Williams's row to the margin and wrote, exception, test more people.

"Saturday," he announced to Aryan at the door. "Park. Bring the Xbox controller if you have to, but leave it in your pocket."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
Chase stood guard over the biggest box of his life: four dozen samosas, two giant jugs of mango juice, and a tray of sweets, all labeled CARGO in his dad's marker. The community hall smelled like onions and excitement, and tomorrow the whole pile would ride in the van at the front of the Vaisakhi procession.

"Watch it," his dad had said. "Last year, half the sweets vanished the night before."

That was the mystery Chase intended to solve. Somebody in this hall was a sweet thief, and he was going to catch them. He recruited the first two people he saw: Kelsey, who lived three houses down, and Edie, who could stare at a wall for ten minutes without blinking, which made her ideal for surveillance work.

"Nobody's getting past me," Edie said, sitting on a folding chair facing the box.

They took shifts while the aunties cooked and the uncles argued about parade route maps. By dinner, the mystery had already begun. The tray of sweets, which Chase had counted twice at eleven in the morning, now held exactly six fewer pieces.

"Somebody's stealing at daylight," he whispered. "Or they're nocturnal. Like a raccoon."

"Raccoons don't like burfi," said Kelsey, who knew this because a raccoon had once rejected her sandwich entirely.

Chase had a plan for the morning. Before anyone touched the cargo, he had laid a thin line of flour across the floor in front of the table, one his dad wouldn't notice. His theory: the thief had to walk, so the thief had to leave tracks. He crouched and squinted at the flour line, and there they were, tiny prints, five toes, raccoon-shaped, leading from the flour to the wall and stopping at a loose vent panel near the floor.

"It IS a raccoon," he said, feeling like a champion detective.

Edie peered at the prints. "Chase. Look at the size of them. That's the biggest raccoon in the world, or..."

Or footprints in socks. Human socks. The prints doubled back and vanished behind the stage curtain.

Chase crept over and yanked the curtain aside. There sat the janitor's kid, a small boy maybe five years old, with flour-socked feet and a burfi crumb on his chin, guarding a tower of stolen sweets like a dragon on gold.

"Twist!" Edie announced, pointing.

They returned the sweets, mostly, except the part that could not be returned for evidence reasons. The little boy's mother promised to keep him away from the cargo, and Chase taped the vent shut anyway, just to be safe.

Outside, the drums were warming up for tomorrow. Kelsey tugged her uncle's sleeve as he carried a banner toward the truck.

"Why does this day matter so much?" she asked him. "Everyone keeps saying it's the big one."

He grinned. "Vaisakhi. In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. That's why the whole city will be out there tomorrow."

"So it's a birthday," Kelsey said.

"Sort of," her uncle said. "Now grab that end of the banner, detective. You too, raccoon catchers."

Chase and Edie each took a corner of the cloth, and the gold letters of the banner snapped open into the evening air.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
The running track circled the hockey rink like a balcony, four laps of hallway carpet above the ice, and in the cold air Payton could hear skates scraping below while the cross-country team warmed up. She had entered her first eight-hundred-metre race on Saturday, and Ms. Okonkwo had let the team use the rink track after practice. Payton's problem was simple and stubborn: both times she had time-trialed the distance, she flew through the first lap and then died on the second, finishing slow and gasping. Something invisible was going wrong, and she meant to find it.

Angela jogged up beside her with the stopwatch. "Want to try again?" she asked. Payton nodded and turned over the paper race number she had pinned to her shirt. On the back, in pencil, she had written her math from the bus that morning: to finish eight hundred metres in three minutes on a four-hundred-metre track, a runner must average ninety seconds for each lap. "So my target is ninety for lap one," Payton said. "Not ninety-five, not eighty. If I hit ninety, I have a shot at three minutes."

The first attempt, she went out hard the way instinct told her to, and Angela called the split at sixty-four seconds. Payton's second lap was one hundred and eleven. "See?" she panted, hands on her knees, watching the zamboni glide below. "Going fast early doesn't conceal the problem. It makes it worse. The fast lap steals from the slow one." Brady, stretching against the railing, grinned. "So don't be a hero for one lap," he said. "Be boring twice."

She tried again, and this time she counted her steps and held back even when her legs begged to sprint. Angela called "ninety-one" at the lap, and Payton kept her rhythm, arms easy, breath even. Coming off the last curve she still had something left, and she spent it all in the final straight. Angela clicked the watch and held it up: three minutes, one second.

"One second off," Payton said, but she was smiling. Brady clapped his mitten-covered hands together. Below them, a goalie tapped his stick on the ice, and the sound rang up through the cold.

"Ninety and ninety-one," Angela said, reading the splits off the watch. "That's the whole secret, isn't it?" Payton folded the race number and put it in her pocket, the pencil numbers facing in. "Ninety and ninety," she said. "On Saturday."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Fox's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn, but nobody mentioned it, because Fox's science project was due Monday and the bean seeds had failed to germinate even though he'd watered them twice a day for two weeks. "They're dead," Fox said, sliding his phone across the table to Samuel. "But that's not my problem. This is my problem."

On the screen was a half-written email: a birthday invitation for Saturday, addressed to exactly one person, Tiana. "I want to invite the whole class," Fox said. "All twenty-six of them. But last time I sent a group email, everybody hit Reply All for three days. Nolan replied 'ok' to twenty-six people. Twice."

Samuel picked up the phone and looked at the fields above the message. To. CC. And under those, a third one, grayed out like it was waiting for something. BCC. He'd seen it a hundred times and never once tapped it. "What's this one do?"

"Blind carbon copy," Fox said, reading the label out loud with a shrug. "No idea. Sounds like a spy thing."

Samuel tapped it anyway. A new field opened up, translucent in the way the phone showed empty boxes, and he typed Tiana's address there instead of in the To line. The To line still needed something, so he put Fox's own address in it. "Test it," he said. "Send that to Tiana and to your mom's account. Then we check what your mom's account shows."

Fox sent it. Then he logged into his mother's laptop at the counter, next to the hummingbird feeder, where a bird was dipping its beak into the nectar so fast it was mostly a blur. The email was there, from Fox, subject and all. Fox's mother's address sat alone in the To line. There was no sign of Tiana anywhere.

"She's invisible," Fox said slowly. "Tiana got it, though. She's already typing."

Samuel scrolled on the laptop and found the proof. Forward, he thought. If somebody forwarded the message, the whole list would come with it, but the list only had one name. Twenty-six people could get the invitation, and no one would see anyone else's address. He felt the idea settle in his chest like a seed that had finally been in the right soil. "Okay. Put every address in BCC. Put your own address in To. Nobody sees anybody."

Fox grabbed the phone and started typing, hunched over the counter while the feeder's sugar water caught the afternoon light. But he stopped halfway through the class list, his thumb hovering above the screen.

"What about Tiana?" he asked. "She told me she doesn't want her address going anywhere. That's why she never signs the group birthday card. She thinks people save them."

Samuel looked at the To line, then at the empty BCC field, and then he grinned. "That's the whole point. She can come, and nobody gets her address. Not even the other kids."

Fox finished the list, double-checked it, and hit Send. The phone buzzed almost immediately with a reply, and he turned the screen so Samuel could see it.

From Tiana: "Saturday. I'll be there. And whatever you just did, tell me how."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Emilia pressed her pencil so hard against the paper that the vanishing point turned into a smudge. She had drawn her street three times already, and every time the shops looked wrong, like the whole block was sliding downhill toward the dot in the middle.

"Ms. Bondarenko's going to pick two drawings for the hallway display on Friday," Jerry said from the next table. He was outlining his bakery again, tracing the same lines over and over so they would look bold. "I want mine chosen so bad my grandma could see it at open house."

"You'll get it," Emilia said, but she was staring at her own paper. Her bakery had a door and two windows, and she had slanted every single edge toward the vanishing point, just like the road. The roofline, the doorframe, even the window tops all leaned inward, and now the front of the building looked like it was toppling over sideways.

Cloe leaned across the aisle. "Whoa. Yours look like they're falling."

"I know," Emilia said. "But the road works, and the roofline works, so why not the windows?" She flipped back to Ms. Bondarenko's example sheet, the one with a neat street and one dot. In the example, the road edges slanted toward the dot, and the rooftops slanted toward it too. But the window tops were flat. So were the tops of the doors. Every line on the fronts of the buildings ran straight across, perfectly horizontal, or straight up and down, perfectly vertical. Emilia's stomach did a small flip. The lines that faced her squarely, straight on, weren't supposed to lean at all. Only the sides of the buildings, the ones angled away, ran toward the vanishing point.

She tested it before she told anyone. On a scrap sheet she drew one shop front with slanted windows and another with flat ones, side by side. The flat one looked solid and calm. The slanted one looked like it was about to precede its own roof into the gutter. She almost laughed out loud.

"Okay, watch," she said to Jerry and Cloe. She erased her window tops, laid her ruler flat, and redrew them horizontal. She squared the doorframes vertical. When she held the paper up, the bakery stood firm at the corner of her street, and the road still raced away toward the dot.

"Whoa," Jerry said. "Show me that again, slow." He had already ruined two windows on his own bakery by slanting them. "Flat for the fronts, angled for the sides."

"Right," Emilia said. "The vanishing point gets the road and the rooftops, but not the fronts."

Cloe frowned at her own paper. "So my whole row of shops has been falling over since Tuesday, and I thought I just couldn't draw." She grinned and started erasing. "Fixing ten windows is not trivial, by the way. You owe me a pencil."

"I'll sharpen you a whole case," Emilia said, and drew her last window, flat and true, while Jerry measured his doorframe twice.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
The stage lights at the community theatre hummed so loudly that Livia could hear them from the wings, where she stood watching Dion fail. He and Calista were supposed to improvise a two-minute scene about a rainy day, and every time Calista said "Yes, and," Dion just nodded and said "Okay" and the scene died like a radio losing signal. Ms. Santoso, who ran the Saturday workshop, clapped her hands and called a break, but Livia barely noticed. She was thinking about last spring, when she had quit the workshop the day before the showcase because she was afraid of freezing in front of a crowd. That fear had sat dormant in her all summer, like something waiting under ice, and she had only just come back.

During the break she wandered past the prop table, where a plastic ship's wheel leaned against a painted backdrop of a spaceship hull, dented and silver. Calista flopped into a folding chair beside her. "Dion keeps stalling," Calista said. "I offer him stuff and he just stands there."

"He's not saying no," Livia said slowly. "He's saying nothing." She turned the ship's wheel with one finger. Something about the prop was snagging in her mind. Last week Ms. Santoso had mentioned a trick in passing, half a sentence tossed over her shoulder, and Livia hadn't caught all of it. Something about how what you say can hand your partner a whole role, like telling them "Doctor, my arm hurts" and suddenly they are the doctor. Livia hadn't understood it then. Now she wondered if the wheel was an answer.

"Can I try a scene with you?" she asked Calista. "Right now, before break ends. I have an idea."

They stepped onto the stage. Livia took a breath and said, "Yes, and it's good thing you showed up, Captain, because the ship's hull is cracked and we're taking on water." She picked up the wheel and held it out.

Calista blinked, then straightened her spine and took it. "Aye. Everyone to stations. And you, First Officer, seal that leak before we lose the cargo." Just like that, Livia was the first officer, and she knew exactly what to do, because Calista's words had made her into it. She knelt by the backdrop and pressed her palms to the painted metal. "Yes, and the sealant is holding, Captain, but there's something moving in the hold."

Dion, watching from the front row, leaned forward. "How did you do that?" he called up. "Calista froze for me every time."

Livia hesitated, half-tempted to keep the trick to herself after how he'd hogged the spotlight in the fall play. But she remembered quitting, and how keeping her fear private had fixed nothing. "It's called endowing," she said. "You give your partner a part through what you say. Watch."

She turned back to Calista. "Captain, we need to disclose what's in that hold before we dock. Should I open it?"

"Open it, First Officer," Calista said. "Whatever's down there has been dormant long enough."
